claims.text: Progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading in FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers is governed by dislocation sources that nucleate preferentially at FCC/BCC interfaces.
Compositional complexity at FCC/BCC interfaces locally reduces the dislocation-nucleation barrier.
Severe lattice distortion at FCC/BCC interfaces locally reduces the dislocation-nucleation barrier.
Local short-range-order variations at FCC/BCC interfaces locally reduce the dislocation-nucleation barrier.
The interfacial compositional and structural variations promote interfacial shear transfer.
The proposed initial coatings contain alternating FCC and BCC high-entropy-alloy layers with individual thicknesses below 100 nm.
The FCC/BCC interfaces act as localized stress concentrators.
Lattice mismatch and compositional fluctuations at the interfaces enhance dislocation nucleation under sustained loading.
Enhanced interfacial dislocation nucleation facilitates intermittent slip events.
Accumulation of interfacial dislocation activity produces progressive plastic strain.
Conventional metallic multilayers exhibit more homogeneous bulk dislocation glide than the proposed high-entropy-alloy multilayers.
High-entropy-alloy multilayers favor a staggered, interface-dominated deformation process.
Relative to conventional metallic multilayers, the high-entropy-alloy multilayers will exhibit more localized deformation at interfaces.
Creep will produce measurable bursts of interfacial dislocation activity.
Creep will produce slight interface sliding.
Creep strain will accumulate non-uniformly across the multilayer.
Layers with greater local lattice misfit or more pronounced short-range-order variations will deform earlier.
Under similar conditions, the high-entropy-alloy multilayers will have a higher creep rate than conventional metallic multilayers.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the nanoscale multilayer architecture is retained and delamination or phase transformation does not occur.
Uniform bulk initiation of plasticity with no correlation between interfaces and dislocation activity would falsify the interface-dominated hypothesis.
